tracks.title: Welcome

segments.text: Welcome to the Alhambra.
This walk starts where your ticket says you must be on time, in the Nasrid Palaces.
From there it moves outward.
First come the council hall, the throne tower and the private Palace of the Lions.
Then the older Partal, and the tower-houses on the walls.
Then across to the Generalife, the summer estate.
Last, back along the old town street to the emperor's palace and the fortress where it all began.
There is one track for each stop.
Each one tells you where to stand, what to look at, and why it matters.
Pause whenever you like.
The building will wait.
I am the second voice.
You will hear me when a story is legend, when experts disagree, or when a detail is widely told but we could not trace it to a solid source.
Inside the palace rooms, please keep your voice down.
The route through the palaces runs one way, and the order of the rooms can change.
If yours differs, follow the signs, and play the track for the room you are in.
Allow four to five hours.
This walk lingers.
When you are ready, make your way to the entrance of the Nasrid Palaces.
Just past the ticket check is the Mexuar.
That is stop one.

tracks.title: The Nasrids in two minutes

segments.text: The Nasrids in two minutes.
Everything in the palaces was built by one family, the Nasrids.
They ruled the last Muslim kingdom in the Iberian peninsula.
In the twelve thirties and twelve forties, the Christian kingdoms of Castile and Aragon were swallowing the great Muslim cities.
Córdoba, Valencia and Seville all fell.
In those same years, one man carved out a kingdom in the mountains around Granada.
His name was Muhammad ibn Nasr, and he ruled as Muhammad the First.
In twelve thirty-eight he started building on this hill.
His kingdom lasted two hundred and fifty years.
It survived by being useful and careful.
Its sultans paid tribute to Castile as vassals.
Sometimes they fought beside it.
When they needed help, they leaned on Morocco.
Granada filled up with Muslims leaving the conquered cities.
It grew rich on silk, on trade and on farming.
So the palaces you are about to see are the luxury of a small state.
It was wealthy, and it was always under threat.
Much of the finest work belongs to just two rulers.
The first is Yusuf the First, who ruled until thirteen fifty-four.
The second is his son, Muhammad the Fifth.
Muhammad the Fifth ruled twice.
He lost the throne in thirteen fifty-nine, won it back three years later, and then ruled until thirteen ninety-one.
You will hear more of that story at stop two.
The end came in fourteen ninety-two.
It followed ten years of war, made worse by civil war inside the ruling family itself.
Keep three names in your ear.
Muhammad the First founded the kingdom.
Yusuf the First and his son, Muhammad the Fifth, built most of what you will see.

tracks.title: How to read a Nasrid wall

segments.text: How to read a Nasrid wall.
This track is for the queue.
Every room in the palaces uses the same vocabulary.
Read each wall from the floor up.
Tiles at the bottom, carved plaster in the middle, wood or honeycomb overhead.
Then the writing, which runs through them all.
Start at the floor.
At eye level and below, the walls are clad in glazed tiles, cut to shape and fitted into geometric patterns.
The Spanish word for this cut tilework is alicatado.
The patterns start simple.
Picture one square.
Lay a second square over it, turned forty-five degrees.
Now you have an eight-pointed star.
Extend its lines, and you get longer stars, octagons and crosses.
Rotate, mirror and repeat.
Choose which lines to keep and which colours to fill.
That is how one square grows into the interlacing star patterns called lazo.
These patterns have had a long afterlife.
The Dutch artist M.
C.
Escher sketched the tiles here in nineteen twenty-two.
He came back to draw them again in nineteen thirty-six.
They fed straight into his interlocking prints.
A century earlier, the architect Owen Jones measured and drew the Alhambra's ornament.
His books, and the Alhambra Court he built at London's Crystal Palace, spread Nasrid patterns through Victorian design.
You will hear that every kind of symmetry is here.
Mathematicians say every repeating flat pattern belongs to one of exactly seventeen types.
The claim is that all seventeen appear on these walls.
Careful surveys disagree, and some count fewer.
Either way, the craftsmen got there centuries before the mathematics was written down.
Why did geometry matter so much?
One historian's answer, in a recent documentary, is that it was useful first.
Astronomy and geometry told people the prayer times and the direction of Mecca.
They guided pilgrims and traders.
They were practical, even religious, skills long before they became an art.
Now the middle band.
Above the tiles, the walls are carved plaster, called stucco.
You will see plant scrolls, lattices, and bands of writing.
Now the ceiling.
It comes in two kinds.
One is carpentry, thousands of small wooden pieces fitted into star patterns.
The other is muqarnas.
These are small, prism-shaped cells of plaster, stacked into honeycomb vaults.
They seem to drip from the dome.
Muqarnas first appeared in the eastern Islamic world, around the tenth and eleventh centuries.
They spread from Iran to Morocco.
Built from a small set of standard shapes, they turn a dome into something like a sky of stars.
That was exactly the effect the Nasrids wanted over a ruler's head.
Often told, though we could not confirm it.
A recent documentary describes the method.
Seven or eight basic prism shapes were cast in plaster moulds.
The pieces were trimmed, polished, and fixed one by one with plaster paste, working upward from the walls.
It is hard to imagine without a written plan, yet no Nasrid drawings survive.
Last, the writing.
Look for a short phrase in a neat frame, repeated again and again.
It is the Nasrid motto, wa-la ghaliba illa Allah.
It means, There is no victor but God.
You will see it so often you stop counting.
Nobody has published a reliable total.
You will hear one figure most of all.
Over nine thousand times.
Treat it as folklore until someone publishes a count.
The story goes that the motto began with the dynasty's founder, Muhammad the First.
Coming home from a campaign, he was hailed as victor.
He answered that there is no victor but God.
His title really was al-Ghalib billah.
But the scene itself is tradition, and accounts disagree on when and where it happened.
Around the motto run verses from the Qur'an, and poems by court poets who were also statesmen.
Ibn Zamrak wrote the poems on the Comares facade and the fountain of the Lions.
Ibn al-Jayyab wrote verses in the Generalife and the Torre de la Cautiva.
A poem in the Throne Room is credited either to him or to Ibn al-Khatib.
Often the building speaks for itself, in the first person.
One window says, I am the fresh eye of this garden.
One myth to drop now.
You will hear that Nasrid art shows no living creatures.
Most of the ornament is abstract.
But wait until you meet twelve stone lions, and a ceiling full of painted kings, knights and ladies.
When the queue moves, follow it through the ticket check.
Just past it is the Mexuar.
That is stop one.

tracks.title: Stop 1. The Mexuar and the Oratory

segments.text: Stop one.
The Mexuar and the Oratory.
You are past the ticket check, inside a long, low hall.
In the middle stand four columns.
At the far end, a small room opens off the hall.
That is the Oratory, the prayer room.
You will end there.
This hall is the Mexuar.
The name comes from the Arabic maswar.
Here the Council of Ministers met, and the sultan gave judgement.
It was built under Isma'il the First, who came to the throne in thirteen fourteen.
In thirteen twenty-five he was murdered by a cousin, inside the palace.
His son, Yusuf the First, and his grandson, Muhammad the Fifth, later redecorated the hall.
It is probably the oldest room in the palaces.
Walk to the four columns in the centre and stand between them.
Look up.
These columns, and the beam they carry, are all that survives of a raised lantern.
It once let light fall into the room from above.
After fourteen ninety-two, the conquerors turned this hall into a chapel.
In the sixteenth century they added an upper floor, and the lantern was lost.
The area behind the balustrade became the choir.
You will read two versions of who lost the lantern.
Some sources say it went under the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella.
Others blame their grandson, Charles the Fifth.
The sources disagree.
Now look down at the tiles along the walls.
Most of the pieces are Nasrid, but Christian tiles are mixed in among them.
Find the eagle with two heads.
That double-headed eagle is the emblem of Charles the Fifth as Holy Roman Emperor.
There it sits, among the Nasrid stars.
It is the first of many places today where the conquerors wrote themselves into the sultans' rooms.
Now raise your eyes to the band of carved plaster just above the tiles.
It reads, The Kingdom is God's, Power is God's, Glory is God's.
This frieze did not start here.
It was salvaged from a lost portico in the courtyard next door, the Court of Machuca.
That court is named after Pedro Machuca, the architect of Charles the Fifth's palace.
He lived there while he built it.
Often told, though we could not find it in a primary source.
Some guides describe another inscription, near the south entrance of this hall.
They say it praises Muhammad the Fifth as the shadow of God over his people.
You will also hear about the excavated foundations you passed on your way in.
They belong to two lost courtyards, thought to have held the chancery and the treasury.
That too is widely repeated, but thinly sourced.
Now walk to the far end of the hall and step into the Oratory.
This small room does not line up with the city wall it sits on.
It is turned toward the qibla, the direction of Mecca.
Ahead of you is the mihrab, the prayer niche.
Now look at the windows.
They sit low.
Worshippers knelt here, so the view of the valley was framed for eyes close to the floor.
The floor itself was lowered in the twentieth century.
Find the inscription that calls out to the passer-by.
It says, Come to pray.
Do not be one of the negligent people.
Much of this room is rebuilt.
In fifteen ninety, a gunpowder store down in the Darro valley exploded.
The blast wrecked the Oratory, which was restored in nineteen seventeen.
You will hear about the same explosion at three more stops.
When you are ready, follow the route out of the Mexuar into a small courtyard with a low fountain.
That is stop two.

tracks.title: Stop 2. Patio del Cuarto Dorado and the Comares facade

segments.text: Stop two.
The Patio del Cuarto Dorado and the Comares facade.
You are in a small courtyard, with a low fountain in the middle.
Facing you is a tall wall, carved from top to bottom.
It has two doorways, and a deep wooden eave at the top.
A room called the Cuarto Dorado, the Golden Room, opens off the courtyard.
This wall is the Comares facade.
It is a political statement in stucco.
Muhammad the Fifth ordered it in thirteen seventy, to celebrate a victory the year before.
Here the public world of the Mexuar met the sultan's private palace.
The sultan sat here, on a raised seat, to receive people.
Look up at the eave.
It is cedar, and it juts out over the courtyard.
It shaded the raised seat below.
Muhammad the Fifth had reason to celebrate.
In thirteen fifty-nine a palace coup drove him from the throne.
He spent nearly three years in exile in Fez, in Morocco.
His vizier, the poet Ibn al-Khatib, stayed beside him.
In thirteen sixty-two he won his kingdom back, with help from Castile.
In the thirteen sixties his court sent the historian Ibn Khaldun as its envoy to Peter the First of Castile, in Seville.
The story goes that Peter the First did more than help.
In thirteen sixty-two he killed the usurper who had driven Muhammad the Fifth out, and he took the usurper's jewels.
One of those jewels, it is said, is the stone called the Black Prince's Ruby.
It now sits in Britain's Imperial State Crown.
That part is legend.
In thirteen sixty-nine Muhammad the Fifth took Algeciras, the port on the Strait of Gibraltar.
That is the victory this wall celebrates.
This facade belongs to his second reign.
So does the redecorated Mexuar behind you, and so does the whole Palace of the Lions.
This is a restored king, building to be seen.
Now find the bands of writing across the facade.
One is a poem by Ibn Zamrak.
Another is the Throne Verse from the Qur'an.
The Throne Verse is among the best-known passages of the Qur'an.
It describes God, ever-living and never sleeping, whose throne extends over the heavens and the earth.
It has long been used as a verse of protection.
Over a ruler's door, it says two things at once.
This house is protected.
And the sultan sits under a far greater throne.
You will often hear the poem quoted as opening, I am a crown on the front of my door.
The gateway speaks for itself.
But the full translation comes only from secondary sites, so treat the wording with care.
Now look at the two doorways, each framed in tile.
They are a lesson in Nasrid privacy.
The right-hand door led to other quarters, possibly a treasury tied to the Mexuar.
The left-hand door leads to the Court of the Myrtles, but not directly.
Its passage bends, so no one standing in this courtyard can see into the palace beyond.
Before you go through, step into the Cuarto Dorado and look up at the cedar ceiling.
Find the pine cones and shells in its pattern.
You will hear two accounts of this ceiling.
It is often credited to the reign of Muhammad the Fifth.
Others say it was repainted and gilded under the Catholic Monarchs.
You will also hear that the low fountain in the courtyard is a copy of one moved here from the Patio de Lindaraja.
Often told, though we could not confirm it.
When you are ready, go through the left-hand door.
Count the turns as the passage bends.
It lets you out into a long courtyard with a pool.
That is stop three.

tracks.title: Stop 3. The Court of the Myrtles

segments.text: Stop three.
The Court of the Myrtles.
The bent passage lets you out into light.
You are in a long, open courtyard.
A narrow pool runs down the middle, with a clipped green hedge along each side.
Those hedges are myrtle, and they give the court its Spanish name, the Patio de los Arrayanes.
Walk to the south end, the end with the wall behind you, and turn around to face north.
Now look up.
The heavy square tower over the far arcade is the Comares Tower.
It is forty-five metres tall, and its walls are thicker than you are tall.
It is a fortress with a throne room inside.
Now look down, at the water.
The tower is there again, upside down.
Crouch near the edge and the whole of it fits in the pool.
That is the trick of this court.
The water is not a fountain.
It is kept almost still, so that it works as a mirror.
It doubles the tower, and it pulls your eye straight down the pool to the place where the sultan sat.
The pool fills almost the whole length of the court, about thirty-four metres.
Walk a few steps beside it and watch the reflection.
It barely trembles.
This was the heart of the official palace.
Here the sultan held court and received foreign envoys.
It was built mainly under Yusuf the First, in the middle of the thirteen hundreds, and redecorated by his son, Muhammad the Fifth.
Yusuf the First died violently.
In thirteen fifty-four, on the feast day of Eid al-Fitr, a madman stabbed him to death while he was at prayer.
Sources differ on where.
Some place it in the Alhambra's own mosque, others in the Great Mosque of the city below.
Two things you will hear in this court.
First, that the name Comares comes from comaraxía, the coloured glass that once filled the tower windows.
That is one theory among several.
The origin of the name is still debated.
Second, and thinly sourced, a story about two restorers.
Rafael Contreras, in the nineteenth century, is said to have put Persian-style domes on these arcades.
Leopoldo Torres Balbás is said to have taken them off again.
We could not confirm that detail for this court.
The argument behind that story is real, and you will meet both names again.
Contreras and his family restored the Alhambra through much of the eighteen hundreds.
They filled gaps with romantic, sometimes invented decoration in what they took to be the Moorish style.
Torres Balbás was the conservation architect from nineteen twenty-three to nineteen thirty-six.
He took a stricter line.
Repair only where there is evidence, and keep new work recognisable.
Much of what you see today is the result of that argument.
When you are ready, walk the length of the pool to the north arcade, under the tower.
That is stop four.

tracks.title: Stop 4. The Sala de la Barca and the Salón de Embajadores

segments.text: Stop four.
The Sala de la Barca and the Salón de Embajadores, the Hall of the Ambassadors.
You are under the north arcade, at the foot of the Comares Tower.
Ahead of you, a double archway leads into a long, narrow room.
That is the Sala de la Barca.
Beyond it, inside the tower itself, is the square throne room.
The throne room may be closed, so follow the signs and go as far as they allow.
Either way, here is what is inside.
Step through the archway into the Sala de la Barca.
It is about twenty-four metres long, and barely wider than a corridor.
Now look up.
The ceiling is curved wood, shaped like the hull of a boat turned upside down.
It is a replica.
The original burned in eighteen ninety, and the replacement was finished in nineteen sixty-four.
You will hear two explanations for the name.
One is that it comes from the Arabic word baraka, meaning blessing, which Castilian ears heard as barca, meaning boat.
The other is that it simply describes the ceiling.
Both are current.
Now walk to the far end, and stand in the doorway of the throne room if you can.
The room is a perfect square.
Look up.
The wooden dome is eighteen metres above you.
It is built from eight thousand and seventeen interlocking pieces of wood.
They form tiers of stars that rise to a single point.
Now find the band of writing at the base of the dome.
These are verses from the Qur'an, from the Surah al-Mulk, the chapter of Sovereignty.
They speak of God who created seven heavens, one above another, and adorned the lowest of them with lamps, the stars.
So the dome is read as an image of those seven heavens.
It is a wooden sky over a fortress room.
Now look at the walls.
There are nine alcoves, three in each side wall.
The middle alcove of the north wall, straight ahead of you, is where the throne stood.
Picture an envoy arriving.
He crossed the bright court, passed through the long Barca, and found the sultan facing him under that sky.
The message was plain.
This throne stands within God's order of the universe, and draws its authority from it.
This hall too was built under Yusuf the First.
A poem in the throne alcove is attributed to one of two court poets, Ibn al-Jayyab or Ibn al-Khatib.
Coloured glass once filled the windows.
Most of it was blown out by an explosion in the Darro valley below, in fifteen ninety.
The Alhambra has a darker place in history.
On the thirty-first of March, fourteen ninety-two, Ferdinand and Isabella signed a decree here.
It expelled Spain's Jews.
It is known as the Alhambra Decree.
An earlier version was dated on the twentieth of March at Santa Fe.
That was the camp-town the monarchs built for the siege of Granada.
The decree gave Spain's Jews until the end of July to convert or leave.
Many tens of thousands left, though the totals are much disputed.
It ended one of the great Jewish communities of medieval Europe.
Granada's Muslims had been promised their faith in the surrender terms.
Within a decade, they too were forced to convert.
You will hear that the decree was signed in this very hall.
That is tradition only.
The documents say simply that it was signed in the Alhambra, and no record names the room.
Often told, though we could not confirm it, is that the dome was once painted, with lapis lazuli among the colours.
We found no technical study to support it.
When you are ready, go back through the Barca into the Court of the Myrtles.
Follow the signs for the route into the Sala de los Mocárabes, the long hall that opens onto the Court of the Lions.
That is stop five.

tracks.title: Stop 5. The Court of the Lions

segments.text: Stop five.
The Court of the Lions.
You begin in the Sala de los Mocárabes, a long entrance hall.
Ahead of you, through the arches, is the brightest court in the palace.
Before you go in, look up.
The vault above you is plaster.
It replaced the original Nasrid honeycomb vaulting, called muqarnas in Arabic.
Its Spanish name, Mocárabes, gives this hall its name.
The original was wrecked by the same explosion of fifteen ninety that blew out the glass of the throne room.
You will hear different dates for this plaster vault.
Some sources say seventeen fourteen, others the sixteen hundreds.
Nobody has settled it.
Now walk into the court.
Stand under the arcade at the near end, the west end.
Line yourself up with the fountain and the far pavilion.
This was the private palace of Muhammad the Fifth, begun around thirteen seventy-seven beside the official palace you have just left.
The court is about thirty-five metres long, and slightly out of square.
A pavilion projects into it at each end.
One is behind you.
The other faces you across the fountain.
The palace is thought to have been called Qasr al-Riyad al-Sa'id, the Palace of the Happy Garden.
That name is often given, but thinly sourced.
Think back to the Court of the Myrtles.
There you had solid walls and still water.
Here you have thin columns and moving water.
Listen for it.
The Myrtles runs north to south.
This court runs east to west, probably because it had to fit between buildings, streets and gardens that were already here.
Yet its two grandest halls still face each other on the north to south line.
The Dos Hermanas is on your left.
The Abencerrajes is on your right.
Now look down at the paving.
Four channels run in from the surrounding halls and meet at the fountain, dividing the court into quarters.
They are usually read as the four rivers of Paradise.
A visitor in fifteen oh two saw six orange trees here, and the rest paved in marble.
Now look at the columns.
There are one hundred and twenty-four of them, in white marble from Macael, in the mountains of Almería.
Those mountains were then part of the kingdom.
Now find a corner of the court.
There the columns bunch together in twos, threes and fours.
The grouping breaks the rhythm of the arcades, so the court reads less like a building and more like a grove of trees.
Some writers find hidden geometry in the plan, based on the square root of two.
Others say the deep eaves block the high summer sun but let the low winter sun into the halls.
Both claims are often told, and thinly sourced.
The fountain carries a poem, carved around the rim of its basin.
It is by Ibn Zamrak, the court poet of Muhammad the Fifth.
His verses say that water and marble are so alike you can hardly tell which one is flowing.
They compare the sultan's generosity to water soaking a garden.
The poem also explains the lions.
You will hear how in the next track.
When you are ready, walk along the channel to the fountain in the centre, and stand by the rim.
Then start the next track.

tracks.title: Stop 5, continued. The twelve lions

segments.text: Stop five, continued.
The twelve lions.
You are standing at the fountain in the centre of the court.
Twelve stone lions stand in a ring, facing outward.
On their backs they carry a twelve-sided basin.
Walk slowly once around them.
Why lions?
Ibn Zamrak's poem on the rim gives the answer.
It likens the flowing water to the ruler's generous hand, and the lions to his warriors.
They look ready to pounce, the poem says, but respect for the emir holds back their fury.
So the fountain is a portrait of power.
Wild strength, tamed and in the sultan's service, pours out water to all four sides of his garden.
On a dry hill, water was the ultimate luxury.
The idea had deep roots in al-Andalus, as Muslim Spain was called.
Four centuries earlier, the Umayyad caliphs of Córdoba built a palace-city, Madinat al-Zahra.
There, a marble basin was ringed by twelve gold animal figures.
A lion was among them.
Muhammad the Fifth liked the motif.
In thirteen sixty-seven he gave his new hospital in the city below, the Maristán, a pair of lion water-spouts.
Those two are now in the museum you will visit later.
Twelve stand here.
Why twelve?
No Nasrid text says.
The number matches the twelve-sided basin and that old model from Córdoba.
Readings of the lions as the zodiac or the months of the year have no evidence behind them.
Often told, though thinly sourced, is that the lions fall into three carving styles, four lions in each.
Look at the manes, the muzzles and the tails, and judge for yourself.
Now listen.
Restorers found that the water once rose through a pierced stone cylinder at the centre.
It slipped out of the lions' mouths almost silently.
It was more like a spring than a fountain.
That matches the poem's picture of water so clear and still that it seems solid.
The fountain has had a busy afterlife.
An upper basin was added in sixteen twenty-six.
It now stands in the Jardín de los Adarves, a garden in the Alcazaba, where you will see it later.
A jet of water rose from the top from eighteen thirty-five until nineteen sixty-six.
During Napoleon's occupation of Granada, from eighteen ten to eighteen twelve, a French commander planted a flower garden in this court.
It was removed in eighteen forty-six, because the damp threatened the building.
In two thousand and seven the lions were taken away for restoration, while the original water system was rebuilt.
They came back at the end of two thousand and eleven.
The restored fountain was unveiled in July twenty twelve.
Most scholars date the lions to the reign of Muhammad the Fifth.
You will hear that the lions are older than this palace.
A theory published in nineteen fifty-six linked them to the Naghrela family.
Samuel ibn Naghrela, and then his son Joseph, were Jewish viziers to the Zirid kings of Granada in the ten hundreds.
Joseph was killed in the massacre of ten sixty-six.
The theory held that the lions came from Joseph's palace.
It rested on a poem by Solomon ibn Gabirol.
The poem describes a basin resting on lions, like the bronze sea carried by twelve oxen in Solomon's Temple.
It is a beautiful idea, but it is disputed.
The carving is fourteenth-century Nasrid work, and most scholars have set it aside.
You may also hear that the fountain worked as a water clock.
That is a guess with no documents behind it.
And one more story we could not confirm, that a traveller in fourteen ninety-four counted thirteen lions here.
When you are ready, follow the channel that runs toward the south side of the court.
If you came in from the west, that is on your right.
Go through the doorway into the square hall.
That is stop six.

tracks.title: Stop 6. The Sala de los Abencerrajes

segments.text: Stop six.
The Sala de los Abencerrajes.
You are in a square hall on the south side of the Court of the Lions.
In the centre is a small marble fountain.
Walk to it and stand beside it.
Now look straight up.
Above you is a dome in the shape of an eight-pointed star.
It is made of muqarnas, honeycomb cells of carved plaster.
The star opens out into eight clusters of hanging points, like stalactites, each one shaped like a tree trunk.
Now find the windows.
There are sixteen, one in each side of the drum that holds up the dome.
They light the honeycomb from within.
The light breaks across the plaster facets, so the ceiling seems to weigh nothing.
Most of this plasterwork was restored in the fifteen hundreds.
Now look down, into the fountain.
It has twelve sides, like the basin outside.
When the water is still, it holds a picture of the dome.
Turn around and find the door you came through.
It is the original wood.
The tiles along the lower walls are later, made in Seville in the fifteen hundreds.
The hall takes its name from the Abencerrajes, a powerful noble family of Nasrid Granada.
And the name comes with a famous legend.
The story goes that the Abencerrajes were invited to a banquet in this hall, and massacred.
The best-known telling is a novel by Pérez de Hita, published in fifteen ninety-five.
In it, a rival clan, the Zegríes, falsely accuse one of the Abencerrajes of an affair with the sultana, Boabdil's wife.
The sultan believes them.
He has the Abencerrajes beheaded here, thirty-six of them in one version.
Versions differ, on the woman, the sultan and the number of the dead.
Some tellings add that the blood still stains the fountain.
It is good storytelling, first written down long after the fall of Granada.
It is not documented history.
Look into the fountain for a reddish stain.
You will hear that it is the blood of the Abencerrajes.
It is usually explained as rust, or iron in the stone.
That is plausible, but we found no study of it.
Behind the legend lies a real feud.
The sultan Muley Hacén, known in Arabic as Abu l-Hasan Ali, fell for Isabel de Solís.
She was a Christian captive who took the name Zoraya.
His passion split the court.
His first wife, Aixa, fled with her sons in fourteen eighty-two.
One of them, Boabdil, rose against his father.
Boabdil would become Muhammad the Twelfth, the last sultan of Granada.
In fourteen eighty-three, Castile captured Boabdil in battle at Lucena, then released him as its vassal.
The civil war that followed, between father, son and uncle, did much to doom the kingdom.
When you are ready, walk back out into the court and turn right.
Follow the arcade to the long hall across the east end.
That is stop seven.

tracks.title: Stop 7. Sala de los Reyes

segments.text: Stop seven.
The Hall of the Kings, the Sala de los Reyes.
You are at the east end of the Court of the Lions.
The long hall in front of you runs behind the arcade and closes this end of the court.
Step inside and walk slowly along it.
As you walk, look up.
Deep alcoves open above you, one after another.
Three of them have curved ceilings, each shaped like a flattened oval.
Stop under the middle one.
These ceilings are not plaster, and they are not wood.
They are leather.
Wet hides were stretched over planed wooden boards shaped into an oval.
Then they were glued, nailed and painted.
In this centre vault, find the ten seated figures.
They are Muslim men, sitting on cushions against a gold ground.
Now look to each end of the same vault.
At each end there are two shields.
They carry the arms of the Order of the Band, a Castilian order of knights.
Now move to one of the side vaults and look up again.
The scene changes completely.
Here are knights and ladies.
Here are hunts, a game of chess, and jousting.
A whole romance of chivalry is painted over your head.
This hall is your proof that the Nasrids were not against images.
In the heart of a Muslim palace, the ceilings are full of human figures.
Who are the ten men in the centre?
Nobody is sure.
The traditional reading is that they are the first ten Nasrid kings, and that reading gave the room its name.
Others see a council, or nobles of the Order of the Band, or Muhammad the Fifth and his court.
If they are kings, the paintings date from about thirteen ninety-six to fourteen oh eight.
The shields are a clue to how tangled the two worlds were.
The Order of the Band was founded by Alfonso the Eleventh of Castile, in the thirteen thirties.
Yet its arms hang over a sultan's hall.
Muhammad the Fifth was a close ally of Peter the First of Castile.
Peter had helped him back to his throne.
In the same years, the thirteen sixties, Peter was building his own palace in the Alcázar of Seville.
He used craftsmen from Granada and from Toledo.
That palace in Seville looks so Nasrid that its plasterwork carries Arabic inscriptions.
They praise a Christian king.
So here you have Christian painters working for a sultan.
In Seville you have Granadan plasterers working for a king.
The frontier was a war zone.
It was also a shared workshop.
Go back to the centre vault and look up once more at the ten figures.
The subjects are Muslim.
But most of the figures, and the buildings painted behind them, look Christian in style.
The painters were probably Christians.
They seem to have had links to a workshop in Toledo, and their work shows touches of Italian painting from the thirteen hundreds.
They were working for a Muslim patron.
Who exactly they were is still debated.
What is certain is what you see.
A Nasrid sultan sat under ceilings full of Muslim figures, painted in the manner of his Christian neighbours.
When you are ready, walk back out into the Court of the Lions.
Cross it to the north side, and go into the hall that opens there, the Hall of the Two Sisters.
That is stop eight.

tracks.title: Stop 8. Dos Hermanas, Ajimeces and the Mirador de Lindaraja

segments.text: Stop eight.
The Hall of the Two Sisters, and the Mirador de Lindaraja.
This is a quiet room.
If you have not gone in yet, you may prefer to hear this track just outside, then step in and look in silence.
You are on the north side of the Court of the Lions, at the door of the Sala de las Dos Hermanas, the Hall of the Two Sisters.
A small fountain sits in the middle of its floor.
Beyond it, a second room, the Sala de los Ajimeces, leads to a little window bay at the far end.
Go in and stand near the fountain.
First, look down.
On either side of the fountain lies a great slab of white marble.
The two slabs match in size and in colour.
They are the two sisters of the name.
Now look up.
Take your time.
The dome above you is muqarnas, a honeycomb of small carved cells.
There are at least five thousand pieces.
The cells cascade from the top in tier after tier, down to an eight-sided drum.
Each side of that drum has two windows.
Sixteen windows in all, letting the light fall through the honeycomb.
Across the court, the Hall of the Abencerrajes has a dome of the same kind.
The two face each other over the Lions.
Together they are the summit of this art.
Now find the bands of writing on the walls.
These are poems, and the room speaks in them for itself.
Here it boasts of its peerless, radiant dome.
You will often hear the opening of this poem translated as, I am a garden graced by every beauty.
It goes on to bring the stars, the moon and Gemini down to touch the dome.
Translations vary, though, and none we found is authoritative.
The poet was Ibn Zamrak.
His verses fill this room and the Lions fountain.
The walls are serene.
His life was not.
Ibn Zamrak was the pupil of the great vizier and historian Ibn al-Khatib.
In thirteen seventy-one, Ibn al-Khatib fled to Morocco.
In Granada his writings were condemned and burned.
In thirteen seventy-four he was put on trial in Fez.
Ibn Zamrak was in the delegation sent from Granada.
Ibn al-Khatib was strangled in prison.
Ibn Zamrak rose to become vizier himself.
In thirteen ninety-three, he too was murdered.
These calm walls were written by men who lived dangerously.
This hall belongs to the private palace of Muhammad the Fifth.
Now walk on through the next room, the Sala de los Ajimeces, to the small window bay at the end.
This is the Mirador de Lindaraja.
Mirador means a place to look out from.
Lindaraja comes from the Arabic ayn dar Aisha, the eye of the house of Aisha.
The window agrees.
Its poem calls it the fresh eye of this garden.
Notice how low the windows sit.
Crouch down, to the height of someone seated on floor cushions.
Now look out.
At this height, the view frames itself.
The room was built for people sitting, not standing.
This bay was the jewel of the private palace.
It once looked out over the Darro valley.
After the Christian conquest, rooms built for Charles the Fifth went up in front of it.
They closed off the view and enclosed the garden below.
One more story about this hall.
A recent documentary says Charles the Fifth dined here during his long honeymoon stay in fifteen twenty-six.
It adds that Pedro Machuca labelled the room His Majesty the Emperor's dining room.
Often told, though we could not confirm it.
When you are ready, follow the route out of these rooms.
It runs along a corridor and down into the garden you just saw below the window.
That is stop nine.

tracks.title: Stop 9. Patio de la Reja, Patio de Lindaraja and the exit

segments.text: Stop nine.
The Patio de la Reja, the Patio de Lindaraja, and the way out.
From the Mirador, the route leads along a corridor.
It passes a small courtyard, the Patio de la Reja, and then goes down into a garden courtyard, the Patio de Lindaraja.
You can listen as you walk.
In the Patio de la Reja, look for a balcony facing the Albaicín and Sacromonte, if it is open on your route.
The rooms along this corridor are not Nasrid.
From fifteen twenty-eight, Charles the Fifth built new rooms here, along a passage linking the Comares palace and the Lions palace.
These are the Emperor's Chambers.
Around fifteen thirty-seven, two painters trained in Raphael's workshop decorated the so-called fruit rooms.
Their names were Julio Aquiles and Alejandro Mayner.
The chambers are normally closed.
They open only now and then, as the Space of the Month.
If the doors are open today, it is worth the detour.
Three centuries after Charles, a famous tenant moved in.
Washington Irving lived in these rooms from the fourth of May to the twenty-ninth of July, eighteen twenty-nine.
A marble plaque on the door of his rooms remembers him.
It was placed there in nineteen fourteen.
When Irving arrived, the Alhambra was half abandoned.
It was a barracks for invalid soldiers, at times a prison, and home to squatters and Gitano families.
His Tales of the Alhambra came out in eighteen thirty-two, and it made the world look again.
Restoration began in earnest in the eighteen forties.
In eighteen seventy the Alhambra was declared a National Monument.
Long before Irving, these palaces were also a royal childhood home.
Catherine of Aragon, later the first queen of Henry the Eighth, spent part of her childhood here.
Sources differ on when her years here began.
She left in fifteen oh one to marry Prince Arthur of England.
Her badge was the pomegranate, the emblem of Granada.
Close by, at the top of a tower, is a small room called the Peinador de la Reina, the Queen's Dressing Room.
It is usually closed too.
Its frescoes, painted in the fifteen forties, show Charles the Fifth's expedition against Tunis.
You will also hear that the Peinador was redecorated for the Empress Isabella in the fifteen hundreds.
That is often told, but thinly sourced.
Now you are in the Patio de Lindaraja.
Turn around and look back up.
Above you is the Mirador, the window bay you just crouched in.
Now you see it from the garden it was named for.
This is the garden that Charles's new rooms closed in.
Stairs from this patio lead to the Comares Baths.
Like the Emperor's Chambers, they are normally closed and open only now and then.
If you do get inside, look up.
The vaults are pierced with star-shaped skylights.
They let the steam out and the air in.
Two things you will hear about these baths.
First, that the resting hall is called the Sala de las Camas, the Hall of the Beds.
The name comes from its two raised benches, where bathers undressed and rested.
Second, that musicians played to the bathers from the gallery of that resting hall.
They are often said to have been blind.
Both details are thinly sourced.
You leave the palaces from this garden, through a gate into the Partal gardens.
If the exit has been moved, follow the staff.
Once you pass the gate, you cannot come back in.
So take a last look.
Listen for the water, and look up once more at the Mirador.
When you are ready, go through the gate and out into the gardens.
That is stop ten.

tracks.title: Stop 10. The Partal: Torre de las Damas, houses, oratory, Partal Alto and the Rauda

segments.text: Stop ten.
The Partal.
This is the start of part two of the tour.
You are in terraced gardens on the north side of the hill.
Below you is a long pool.
Beyond it stands a portico of five arches, and behind that a tower, the Torre de las Damas.
Walk to the far end of the pool, and turn to face the arches.
Look down.
The five arches are reflected in the water.
It is the idea of the Court of the Myrtles, at an earlier, simpler stage.
This is the oldest palace still standing in the Alhambra, though only part of it stands.
Its style suggests it was built under Muhammad the Third, early in the thirteen hundreds.
Partal comes from the Arabic al-Bartal, from the Latin for portico.
The palace is named after the very thing in front of you.
Now look at the arches.
Above them, the stucco forms a lattice, a net of interlacing lines.
Below, slender marble columns hold them up.
Those columns date only from nineteen sixty-five.
They are the work of Francisco Prieto-Moreno, who succeeded Torres Balbás.
Brick pillars first held up these arches.
Some sources go further, and say that only the central arch of the portico is original.
We could not confirm it.
If you go into the tower, look up at where the ceiling should be.
The original carved wooden dome is in Berlin.
The Tower of the Ladies is only a nineteenth-century nickname.
Its last private owner was the German banker Arthur von Gwinner.
He removed the dome before giving the building to the Spanish state in eighteen ninety-one.
Since nineteen seventy-seven it has belonged to Berlin's Museum of Islamic Art.
Next to the tower, raised on the wall, is a small oratory, a prayer room.
Its prayer niche, the mihrab, faces the correct direction.
The oratory is usually credited to Yusuf the First.
But its timber has been tree-ring dated to thirteen thirty-two or thirty-three.
That suggests Ismail the First may have begun it.
Along the wall runs a row of small Nasrid houses.
Look in if any are open.
One of them, the House of the Paintings, keeps rare wall paintings from the thirteen hundreds.
Found in nineteen oh seven, they show rows of horsemen, and tents with musicians, servants and women of the Nasrid court.
Now look uphill, above the gardens.
There is the excavated outline of another palace.
Find the long pool, the footings of rooms, and the remains of a bath.
This is the Partal Alto, the upper Partal.
It was long called the Palace of Yusuf the Third.
Current scholarship gives it to an earlier sultan, Muhammad the Second, in the late twelve hundreds.
After the conquest of fourteen ninety-two, it became the home of the Count of Tendilla, the Christian governor of the Alhambra.
His descendants, the Marquises of Mondéjar, held the governorship almost as an inheritance for two centuries.
Then they backed the losing side in the War of the Spanish Succession.
In seventeen seventeen the winner, Philip the Fifth, stripped them of office.
The Marquis then pulled the palace down and sold off pieces.
Sources differ on whether that was in seventeen eighteen or in the seventeen thirties.
The site was excavated in nineteen twenty-four.
About a third of it is still buried.
One more place belongs to this story, though you cannot see it from here.
The sultans were buried in a royal cemetery called the Rauda.
It lay just across the lower street, the Calle Real Baja, from the royal palaces.
You will pass close to its site later.
Ismail the First, Muhammad the Fourth, Yusuf the First and Yusuf the Third were buried there, and probably Muhammad the Fifth.
After the conquest, Boabdil dug up his ancestors and took them with him into exile.
They probably went to a burial ground his wife owned, at Mondújar.
When the Rauda was excavated in nineteen twenty-five, about seventy tombs were found.
All but one were empty.
No remains of the dynasty survive.
When you are ready, walk east along the path inside the northern wall, with the wall on your left.
That is stop eleven.

tracks.title: Stop 11. Paseo de las Torres

segments.text: Stop eleven.
The Paseo de las Torres, the walk of the towers.
This begins part three of the tour.
You are on the path that runs east from the Partal, just inside the northern wall.
Keep the wall on your left.
At intervals, towers jut out from it.
You will pass them one by one on your way toward the Generalife.
Start walking, and listen as you go.
These towers were homes as well as defences.
A military tower fitted out as a home had its own name in Arabic, qalahurra, a tower-palace.
In Spanish it became calahorra.
The first you come to is the Torre de los Picos.
Look up at its pointed battlements.
It guarded the Puerta del Arrabal, a gate leading down toward the Albaicín.
Inside, it has three vaulted levels, decorated with stucco and paintings.
Its date is disputed.
The first tower may go back to around thirteen hundred, with later work under Yusuf the First and Muhammad the Fifth.
Walk on.
Next comes the Torre del Cadí, and after it the Torre de la Cautiva.
From outside, the Cautiva looks like any other tower.
Inside, it is second only to the Comares Tower in richness.
It is credited to Yusuf the First, who made it a home.
It was finished before thirteen forty-nine, possibly on top of an earlier tower.
Its tile poems are by Ibn al-Jayyab.
One inscription sums up the whole idea.
It calls the tower a calahorra with a palace within, a fortress and a mansion to be enjoyed.
About that name.
Cautiva means captive, and you will hear it called the Tower of the Captive.
It is a fanciful name with no historical basis.
The story that links it to Isabel de Solís is legend.
The Cautiva and the Picos open from time to time as the Space of the Month.
If you find a door open, go in.
Now walk on, farther east, to the Torre de las Infantas, the Tower of the Princesses.
It was built, or rebuilt, by Muhammad the Seventh toward the end of the thirteen hundreds.
This tower shows how such homes stayed bearable in a Granada summer.
The main rooms face north, away from the sun.
The earthen walls are so thick that the day's heat takes hours to get through.
The windows are small and screened with lattices.
High openings let rising hot air escape.
Water in the central basin cools the air as it evaporates.
Along this stretch, the defensive wall became a string of private apartments with views.
It is the idea of the Comares Tower, on a smaller scale.
A few things you will hear along this wall.
First, that the Infantas is the setting of Washington Irving's Legend of the Three Beautiful Princesses, in his Tales of the Alhambra.
Second, a recent documentary claims that rooms like these stayed around twenty-five degrees while it was forty outside.
It also says Nasrid watchtowers across the kingdom passed warnings to the Alhambra by smoke and mirror signals.
Both are plausible, but we could not check either.
Third, the Torre del Agua, the Water Tower, farther on, is a ruin.
The story goes that Napoleon's troops blew it up as they withdrew in eighteen twelve.
Guides also say that the royal water channel, the Acequia Real, crosses into the Alhambra there on a small aqueduct, and that the tower was built to guard it.
And the path outside the wall, the Camino de Ronda, is often called a patrol path or a moat.
None of this is firmly sourced.
Your next stop is the Generalife.
The old way in was near the Torre del Agua, across the ravine of the Cuesta del Rey Chico.
Rey Chico means the little king.
It is what the Castilians called Boabdil.
Today, follow the signs across the bridge by that tower.
Allow roughly ten to fifteen minutes.
That is stop twelve.

tracks.title: Stop 12. The gardens and the water

segments.text: Stop twelve.
The gardens and the water.
This is the Generalife, the sultans' country estate on the hill facing the Alhambra.
It has its own signed, one-way route.
Follow it, and take the next stops in whatever order it gives you.
You are in the new gardens below the palace.
Around you are hedged walks, walls of clipped cypress and long pools, and an open-air theatre.
Now look ahead and up the slope.
The building above you is the summer palace.
These gardens are not medieval.
They are the Jardines Nuevos, the New Gardens, laid out between nineteen thirty-one and nineteen fifty-one by the restorers Torres Balbás and Prieto-Moreno.
The theatre followed in nineteen fifty-two.
Now look down the slope.
The terraced orchards there have been farmed since the thirteen hundreds.
The Generalife was never only a garden.
It was an almunia, a country estate that was both a retreat and a working farm, a short walk from the palace.
It probably began under Muhammad the Second, at the end of the twelve hundreds.
An inscription records that Isma'il the First remodelled it in thirteen nineteen.
Yusuf the Third reworked the southern parts in the fourteen hundreds.
Another inscription, by Ibn al-Jayyab, calls the estate the House of the Felicitous Kingdom.
Now listen.
Wherever you stand on this estate, you can hear water moving.
All of it arrives by gravity.
Here is how, in three steps.
First, the source.
Far up the valley, about six kilometres upstream, a channel takes water from the river Darro.
That channel is the Acequia Real, the royal channel.
It runs gently downhill along the side of the valley, all the way here.
Second, the split.
Several kilometres before the estate, a smaller channel branches off.
This is the Acequia del Tercio.
It runs along higher ground, to feed the upper gardens and the Water Stairway.
The main channel stays lower, and runs right through the palace above you.
Third, the join.
Past a medieval reservoir called the Albercones, the two channels meet again.
Together they go on to the Alhambra.
They enter it by the Water Tower, the Torre del Agua, and fill its pools and fountains.
So, one river.
A high channel and a low channel.
One slow slope across a whole valley.
That is the engine behind every pool and fountain you have seen on this hill.
Now look up, to the hilltop above the estate.
The ruined fort up there is the Silla del Moro.
It was a lookout, and one of its jobs was to guard this water supply.
Often told, thinly sourced.
A recent documentary describes very deep wells on the hill above the Generalife.
In them, it says, waterwheels turned by animals lifted water further uphill, in stages.
Treat the details as approximate.
The same programme claims the Nasrids had a pressure device that pushed water up to the Alcazaba, and that nobody else in medieval Iberia could do it.
We found nothing to support this.
Treat it with real caution.
And a myth check on the name.
You will hear that Generalife comes from the Arabic Jannat al-'Arif, the Garden of the Architect.
Scholars dispute this, and other readings have been proposed.
When you are ready, follow the signed route up through the gardens to the palace entrance.
Beyond it lies a long courtyard with water running down the middle.
That is stop thirteen.

tracks.title: Stop 13. Patio de la Acequia and the Sala Regia

segments.text: Stop thirteen.
Patio de la Acequia and the Sala Regia.
You have come through the palace entrance into a long, narrow courtyard.
A channel of water runs down its whole length, with planted beds on either side and a pavilion at each end.
This is the Patio de la Acequia, the Court of the Water Channel.
Walk to the south end and turn to face north, toward the taller pavilion.
Now stand still and listen.
Under the splash of the fountains there is a lower, steadier sound.
It is the channel itself, running past your feet.
This is the royal channel from the last stop.
The same water goes on to feed the whole Alhambra.
The arcing jets are pretty, but they were added in the eighteen hundreds.
Picture the court the Nasrid way.
No jets.
Plants at the level of your feet.
Only that quiet running sound down the middle.
How do we know?
After a fire in nineteen fifty-eight, excavations found the Nasrid garden about seventy centimetres below today's beds.
The original beds were sunken below the paths.
They were planted low, with plants like myrtle, and had deeper pits for orange trees.
The old level was then covered over and replanted.
Garden historians read all this water as a statement of royal power and good stewardship.
There may be no water on this hill, but the sultan has it.
He uses it to make the land fruitful, as a good Muslim ruler should.
Unlike the palaces across the ravine, the Generalife had no grand state rooms.
It was a place for the court's pleasure, close enough for a day trip.
Now turn to your left, to the western wall.
Halfway along, a small room juts out.
That is a mirador, a room built to frame a view.
It is probably the earliest known mirador in Nasrid architecture.
Step inside and look back across the ravine.
The Alhambra is in front of you.
Rooms like this one are the forerunners of the Mirador de Lindaraja in the palaces.
Now walk to the north pavilion and look up.
The upper gallery was added by the Catholic Monarchs in fourteen ninety-four, two years after the conquest.
Below it, find the entrance with three arches in carved stucco.
It leads into the Sala Regia, the royal hall.
The inscriptions around it are by Ibn al-Jayyab.
Go in and look up, at the wooden ceiling and the frieze of muqarnas, the honeycomb carving.
Another mirador projects from this hall, looking toward the Albaicín.
Isma'il the First added it in thirteen nineteen.
The estate outlived the sultans.
After the conquest, the Generalife passed to the Granada-Venegas family, descendants of a Nasrid prince who had converted.
They and their heirs held it for about four centuries.
Then came a long lawsuit.
It ended in a settlement, and in nineteen twenty-one the estate was handed to the Spanish state.
You will hear this about the north portico.
Beside its entrance are two small wall niches, called tacas.
They are said to have held jars of cool water.
An inscription attributed to Isma'il the First is said to compare them to maidens greeting guests.
We could not confirm its wording.
When you are ready, follow the route up from this court to the next courtyard, the Court of the Sultana's Cypress.
That is stop fourteen.

tracks.title: Stop 14. Patio del Ciprés de la Sultana, the Water Stairway and the Mirador Romántico

segments.text: Stop fourteen.
The Patio del Ciprés de la Sultana, the Water Stairway, and the Mirador Romántico.
You are above the Patio de la Acequia, in a courtyard of pools and clipped hedges.
This is the Court of the Sultana's Cypress.
Paths lead on from here, up to the upper gardens.
Find the arcade on the north side.
It was built between fifteen eighty-four and fifteen eighty-six.
This whole courtyard was designed after the Nasrids had gone.
The courtyard takes its name from a legend.
The story goes that a sultana was caught here, meeting a knight of the Abencerraje family under a cypress.
The discovery led to the downfall of that family.
It is the same family as in the palace legend.
Whose wife was she?
In most tellings she is Morayma, the wife of Boabdil.
Other tellings make her the wife of Muley Hacén.
Versions differ.
Treat all of it as legend.
You will also hear that the famous cypress itself is long dead, and that its trunk is kept as a relic of the story.
That too is often told and thinly sourced.
Now leave the courtyard and follow the paths uphill to the Water Stairway, the Escalera del Agua.
It climbs the slope under a canopy of laurels.
At the foot of the stairs, stop.
Put your hand on the handrail and feel along the top.
It is an open channel.
Water is running down it, right beside your fingers.
Now stand still and listen.
On both sides of you, the rails are running.
As you climb, the water slides down past you toward the palace.
Start to climb.
The flights break at small round landings, each with a fountain.
Pause at each one and listen to the change in sound.
This stairway existed in the Muslim period, and it is reputedly the oldest stair in these gardens.
Its water comes from the higher channel, the Acequia del Tercio, the branch that splits off far up the valley.
Here, at last, you can put your hand in it.
Often told, thinly sourced.
The stairway is often linked to the poet Juan Ramón Jiménez, who is said to have written about its running handrails.
At the top stands the Mirador Romántico, the Romantic Lookout, built in eighteen thirty-six.
It probably stands on the site of a former prayer hall.
Go to the edge and look out.
From here you can read the whole water system.
Below you runs the channel.
Then come the palace and its courtyards, and the orchards on the slope.
Across the ravine is the Alhambra, where all this water is heading.
When you are ready, follow the signed exit route out of the Generalife.
Cross back over the bridge by the Torre del Agua, the Water Tower, into the Alhambra, and stop at the start of the main street.
That is stop fifteen.

tracks.title: Stop 15. Along the Calle Real

segments.text: Stop fifteen.
Along the Calle Real.
You are back inside the walls of the Alhambra.
Behind you is the bridge by the Torre del Agua, where the royal channel enters.
Ahead of you, running west, is the Calle Real, the Royal Street.
It was the main street of the old palace town, the Medina.
At the far end, ahead, is the great square block of the Palace of Charles the Fifth.
Start walking toward it, at your own pace.
This was a town serving a court, not just a palace.
It had its own mosque, its own baths, and its own royal cemetery.
Partway along, you reach the Church of Santa María de la Alhambra.
It was built between fifteen eighty-one and sixteen eighteen, on the site of the Alhambra's main mosque.
Muhammad the Third commissioned that mosque, and it was finished in thirteen oh five.
It was pulled down in fifteen seventy-six.
Yusuf the First, builder of the Comares palace, was stabbed to death at prayer on the feast of Eid al-Fitr in thirteen fifty-four.
Sources differ on whether it happened in the mosque that stood here, or in the Great Mosque down in the city.
Now look to your right, down the lower street.
That is the Calle Real Baja.
Near it lay the Rauda, the royal cemetery.
The sultans' tombs lay just north-west of the mosque.
Often told, thinly sourced.
Near the church is a small Nasrid bathhouse, the Baño de la Mezquita, the Bath of the Mosque.
It is listed as free to enter when it is open.
The Catholic Monarchs were first buried on this hill.
Queen Isabella died in fifteen oh four and was laid to rest in the convent of San Francisco, just off this street.
That building is now the Parador hotel.
Ferdinand joined her there in fifteen sixteen.
In fifteen twenty-one, both were moved down to the Royal Chapel in the city.
If you have five minutes, there is a detour.
From the Calle Real, walk a short way downhill to the southern wall.
There stands the Puerta de los Siete Suelos, the Gate of the Seven Floors.
It is a gate of Yusuf the First, from the thirteen hundreds.
It has a bent entrance, and a bastion added after the conquest.
Despite the name, excavations have found only two levels below ground.
The legend says Boabdil rode out through this gate in fourteen ninety-two.
He begged that no one ever pass through it again, and so it was walled up.
History adds a darker chapter.
In September eighteen twelve, Napoleon's troops were abandoning Granada.
As they left, they blew up this gate, along with other towers on the south wall.
It was later rebuilt.
Worse was planned.
A plaque honours José García, a corporal of the invalid soldiers' corps.
In that same year he risked his life to save the palaces and towers from ruin.
The usual telling has him cutting the burning fuses.
The plaque itself gives no details.
When you are ready, return to the Calle Real and keep walking west.
Go around the palace to the open esplanade in front of its west front.
That is stop sixteen.

tracks.title: Stop 16. Palace of Charles V

segments.text: Stop sixteen.
The Palace of Charles the Fifth.
You are on the open esplanade, facing the west front of a vast square palace.
It belongs to a different world from everything else on this hill.
This is the Renaissance, set down in a Nasrid palace city.
The front is sixty-three metres wide.
The whole building is a square of that size.
Look at the lower storey.
The stone is left rough and heavy, in deep blocks.
This is called rusticated stone.
Now look up, to the upper storey.
Here the columns are Ionic, lighter and smoother.
Now look closely at the flat pillars of the lower storey.
Set into them are bronze rings.
Find the doorways.
They are framed in stone from Sierra Elvira.
On the facade, look for a carved battle scene.
It shows the Battle of Pavia, in northern Italy, in fifteen twenty-five.
There Charles's army crushed the French and captured King Francis the First himself.
It was the high point of his power, and he had it carved onto his palace here.
Several things are said about this front.
The main west portal is said to have been finished under Philip the Second by Juan de Herrera.
The facades are said to carry green marble medallions, and reclining winged figures above the doorways.
Treat these as unconfirmed.
You will also notice that the palace sits at a slight angle to its neighbours.
One story says the archbishop objected to it crowding the church on the site of the old mosque.
That too is unconfirmed.
Who built this, and why here?
Charles the Fifth was the grandson of Ferdinand and Isabella.
He was king of Spain from fifteen sixteen and Holy Roman Emperor from fifteen nineteen.
He ruled much of Europe and the Americas.
In fifteen twenty-six he married Isabella of Portugal in Seville.
He then spent several months in the Alhambra, and decided to build a second royal residence here.
The designer was Pedro Machuca, trained in Rome.
Work began in fifteen twenty-seven.
Machuca directed it on site from fifteen thirty-three until his death in fifteen fifty.
His son Luis built the courtyard.
Charles never lived in it.
Neither did his son, Philip the Second, who moved the court to Madrid.
Work stopped for fifteen years after the Morisco rebellion of fifteen sixty-eight.
In sixteen thirty-seven it was abandoned without a roof.
Restoration began in nineteen twenty-three, and the building was finished only in the middle of the twentieth century.
It is often said that a special tax paid by the Moriscos largely funded the work.
Who were the Moriscos?
After fourteen ninety-two, Granada's Muslims were promised freedom of religion.
Between fourteen ninety-nine and fifteen oh two, they were forced to choose baptism or exile.
Those who stayed became Moriscos, Christians in name only.
Step by step, their language, dress and customs were banned.
In fifteen sixty-eight that pressure exploded in a great revolt in the Alpujarras.
Those are the valleys on the far side of the Sierra Nevada, the mountains you saw from the Alcazaba.
The revolt was crushed, and Granada's Moriscos were scattered across Castile.
Between sixteen oh nine and sixteen fourteen they were expelled from Spain altogether.
This half-built palace is, among other things, a monument to that story.
Now walk inside, to the courtyard.
You are standing in a circle, about thirty metres across, set inside the square.
Two rings of columns run around you.
Doric below, plain and sturdy.
Ionic above.
A circle inside a square was a Renaissance ideal.
Machuca split the plan along a diagonal, into an emperor's side and an empress's side.
Each had its own staircase, and the two met at an eight-sided chapel.
Walk to the centre and look up at the open sky.
Now think back to the Court of the Lions.
That court is all columns and light.
This one is all mass.
Try this.
Stand dead centre and speak or clap softly.
Many visitors notice an echo.
You will also hear this court compared to Hadrian's Villa at Tivoli.
And one famous line.
Charles is often quoted as saying, on first seeing the Alhambra, unfortunate the man who lost all this.
No early source records it.
When you are ready, follow the signs to the Alhambra Museum.
That is stop seventeen.

tracks.title: Stop 17. The Alhambra Museum and the Vase of the Gazelles

segments.text: Stop seventeen.
The Alhambra Museum and the Vase of the Gazelles.
You are on the ground floor of the Palace of Charles the Fifth, inside the Alhambra Museum.
This floor holds the Nasrid collection, the objects made and used by the sultans' court.
The Fine Arts Museum, the Museo de Bellas Artes, is on the floor above you.
Make your way through the galleries to room five.
It is the room with the low lights.
Find the tall jar in blue and gold.
Follow its outline with your eyes, from the foot, up the swelling body, to the neck.
This is the Vase of the Gazelles.
It was made under Muhammad the Fifth, a sultan you have met many times on this walk.
Many large jars of this kind once stood in the palaces.
This is the only one that keeps its full curved outline.
It is also the only one that has never left the Alhambra.
Now look for the gazelles that give the jar its name.
They are picked out in gold, among the blue.
The gold is not paint and it is not metal leaf.
It is lustre, a glaze that shines like metal.
Lustre takes three firings in the kiln.
The last firing is done with the air starved of oxygen.
That turns a thin coating of copper and silver into a metallic sheen that sits on the surface of the glaze.
Golden lustreware like this was a prized product of Nasrid Granada.
It was exported from Málaga, the kingdom's port on the coast.
The jar has moved around the Alhambra for centuries.
It stood in the Jardín de los Adarves, in the Court of the Myrtles, in the Hall of the Kings, and in the Hall of the Two Sisters.
Then it came here.
You will walk through that first garden later, in the fortress.
Two things guides often tell you about this jar.
First, a tip.
The room is kept dim on purpose.
Stand still, and move your head slowly from side to side.
The lustre catches the light, and the gazelles come up in gold.
It costs nothing to try.
Second, you will often hear that the vase is about one metre thirty-five tall, and that it was made in Málaga.
Both are plausible.
But the museum itself does not confirm either one, so treat them as likely, not certain.
Before you leave, look for the royal tombstones.
They come from the Rauda, the royal burial ground of the Nasrid sultans.
Find the carved Arabic writing on their faces.
These stones once marked the graves of the men who built the palaces you have just walked through.
One more thing for later.
At the end of the walk, on the Gate of Justice, you will see a carved Virgin and Child.
That one is a copy.
The original is upstairs, in the Fine Arts Museum.
When you are ready, leave the palace and walk west.
Ahead, at the edge of a wide open square, a gate stands on its own.
That is stop eighteen.

tracks.title: Stop 18. Puerta del Vino and the Plaza de los Aljibes

segments.text: Stop eighteen.
Puerta del Vino and the Plaza de los Aljibes.
This begins the last part of the walk, the Wine Gate and the fortress.
Allow most of an hour for it.
The Palace of Charles the Fifth is behind you.
Ahead, a gate stands on its own at the edge of a wide open square.
This is the Puerta del Vino, the Wine Gate.
You are looking at its east face.
Later you will walk around to the other side.
Take in the gate as a whole first.
It has two levels.
Below is a stone passage under a horseshoe arch.
Above it sits a room built of brick.
Now look at the curved spaces on either side of the arch.
They are filled with tiles.
Leaves and branches in green, blue and yellow wind across a white ground.
Above them, a stucco frame surrounds the upper window.
Look for traces of old paint, and for the reddish brickwork.
This decoration is later than the gate itself.
It was added about half a century after the gate was built.
The gate dates from the early thirteen hundreds.
It is usually credited to Muhammad the Third, though some sources point to Muhammad the Second.
This was the main entrance to the Medina, the town on the hill.
Today the gate stands alone, but it may once have stood among buildings that have since gone.
Now walk through the passage to the west face, and turn around to look at it.
Look just above the arch.
A key is carved there, hanging from a cord.
Keep it in mind.
You will meet the same key again at the end of the walk, on the Gate of Justice.
Nobody is sure what the key meant.
It may be a sign of power, to open and to close.
It may stand for faith as the key to paradise.
Or it may simply be a Nasrid emblem.
Whatever it meant, it marked an official gateway.
Now find the Arabic plaque on this face.
It honours the sultan Muhammad the Fifth.
Now turn to the square.
You are standing on water.
Plaza de los Aljibes means the Square of the Cisterns.
This was once a gully between the fortress and the palaces.
In fourteen ninety-four, two years after the conquest, the Count of Tendilla built cisterns in it.
They are thirty-four metres long and eight metres deep.
Later the gully was filled in, and the square was laid on top.
Flamenco history was made on this square.
On the thirteenth and fourteenth of June, nineteen twenty-two, it hosted the Concurso de Cante Jondo, a contest of deep song.
Deep song is the oldest layer of flamenco singing.
The contest was organised by the composer Manuel de Falla and the young poet Federico García Lorca.
They feared the old style was dying out.
Falla has another link to this gate.
In late nineteen oh nine, he sent the French composer Debussy a postcard of it.
Myth check, on two points.
First, the name.
You will hear that it is the Wine Gate because residents could bring wine in here without paying tax.
That right is recorded in the middle of the fifteen hundreds, though accounts disagree on the exact year.
Or the name may be a garbling of an older Arabic one.
Nobody knows which.
Second, Debussy.
You will hear that he wrote his piano prelude, La Puerta del Vino, after seeing this gate.
He never saw it.
The prelude, from nineteen thirteen, was sparked by that postcard from Falla.
If you need them, toilets, lockers and first aid are close to this gate.
When you are ready, cross the square to the fortress walls.
The entrance to the Alcazaba is from this square.
That is stop nineteen.

tracks.title: Stop 19. The Alcazaba

segments.text: Stop nineteen.
The Alcazaba.
You are at the entrance to the Alcazaba, the fortress on the western tip of the hill.
Follow the marked route through it.
This is where the Alhambra began.
Muhammad the First, founder of the Nasrid dynasty, started building here in twelve thirty-eight, on the site of an older castle.
In the eleventh century, Granada was ruled by the Zirid kings.
Their chief ministers were a Jewish father and son, Samuel ibn Naghrela and Joseph.
Joseph was killed in ten sixty-six, in a massacre of the Jews of Granada.
A disputed point.
One scholar placed Joseph's palace here, on this hill.
Not everyone accepts it.
Put your hand on the wall if you can reach it.
This is rammed earth.
Look for rows of small square holes.
Builders packed earth, lime and gravel into wooden frames, one layer at a time.
The holes mark where the crossbeams of those frames sat.
These plain, thick walls are the reason the palaces could be all lace and light.
Walk into the Jardín de los Adarves, the narrow garden along the southern ramparts.
This garden was once a moat, between the outer and inner walls.
In the sixteen hundreds the governor, the Marquis of Mondéjar, had it filled and planted.
The Vase of the Gazelles stood here once.
So did the upper basin of the Lions fountain.
Find that basin now.
Walk on to the west end of the garden, to the Torre de la Pólvora, the Powder Tower.
Look for a plaque on its wall.
The lines on it are by the Mexican poet Francisco de Icaza.
In English they read: Give him alms, woman, for there is nothing in life like the grief of being blind in Granada.
A local legend says this garden was paid for with gold coins, found hidden in jars inside the walls.
It is only a legend.
Now follow the route into the Plaza de Armas, the parade ground.
Look down at the low walls at your feet.
These are the foundations of the Barrio Castrense, the soldiers' quarter.
Trace the outlines of houses, a bakery, a bath, a cistern and workshops.
Below them lie silos and dungeons, cut underground.
At the eastern end stands the keep, the Torre del Homenaje.
It guarded the main entrance.
It is about twenty-six metres high, with five vaulted floors.
Tradition says the founder lived on its top floor.
At the western prow stands the Torre de la Vela.
These two are the oldest towers of the fortress.
Vela means watch, and that was its job.
After the earthquakes it may be closed, so follow the signs, and climb it if it is open.
Look up at its bell.
Bell registers date the present bell to seventeen seventy-three.
It seems to have been set in its present position in eighteen forty, and it was rebuilt after lightning damage in eighteen eighty-two.
The bell told farmers on the plain below when their turn came to take irrigation water at night.
It also served as a clock and an alarm.
Today it rings only on set days, such as the second of January.
Folklore says that a single woman who rings it on that day will marry within the year.
The gunpowder blast in the Darro valley in fifteen ninety damaged this tower too.
It was repaired the same year.
A few more things you will hear, all thinly sourced.
After the conquest, the Count of Tendilla is said to have adapted the fortress for cannon.
The rounded bastion by the Powder Tower is the usual example.
Another tower, the Torre de las Armas, is said to have linked the fortress to the Albaicín by a bridge over the river.
We could not confirm these.
Now walk out onto the ramparts, or the terrace of the Puerta de las Armas, and look out.
Across the Darro valley, on the next hill, is the old quarter of the Albaicín.
To the west, the city spreads out into the Vega, the farming plain.
On a clear day, turn around.
The Sierra Nevada rises behind you.
Stay here on the ramparts for the next track.
That is stop nineteen, continued.

tracks.title: Stop 19, continued. The fall of Granada

segments.text: Stop nineteen, continued.
The fall of Granada.
Stay on the ramparts.
The Torre de la Vela, the watchtower with the bell, is at the western prow of the fortress.
Find it now.
This is where the Nasrid kingdom ended.
Granada was not taken by storm.
Its end was negotiated.
On the twenty-fifth of November, fourteen ninety-one, the two sides signed the Capitulations of Granada.
These were the terms of surrender.
They promised the Muslims of Granada their faith, their property and their own laws.
Those promises were broken within ten years.
On the second of January, fourteen ninety-two, the last sultan, Boabdil, handed over the city to Ferdinand and Isabella.
That same day, their banners were raised on the Torre de la Vela, in front of you.
Tradition places the handing over of the keys down by the river Genil, below the city.
A small chapel stands there, the Ermita de San Sebastián.
One visitor was still waiting for an answer.
Christopher Columbus was in Granada, hoping for royal backing for a voyage west.
He got it that April.
He later wrote that he had seen the royal banners planted by force of arms upon the towers of the Alhambra.
Now turn south, toward the mountains.
That is the way Boabdil rode into exile.
The story goes that he stopped on a mountain pass for a last look at Granada, and wept.
His mother, Aixa, is said to have told him to weep like a woman for what he had not defended like a man.
The pass is still called the Suspiro del Moro, the Moor's Sigh.
But treat the scene as legend.
It was first written down in the fifteen thirties, about forty years later, and even then only as hearsay.
Now look down at the walls under your feet, and the towers around you.
Notice their colour, a dull, warm red.
That colour gave the whole place its name.
In Arabic, al-Hamra means the red one.
These rammed earth walls were made with local clay rich in iron oxide.
Over the centuries, al-Hamra became Alhambra.
You will also hear a second explanation, often told alongside the first.
Muhammad the First, who founded this fortress, was known as Ibn al-Ahmar, the son of the red one.
Some link the name of the Alhambra to him as well.
That link is thinly sourced.
The colour of the walls is the better supported explanation.
Take a last look at the view.
Then you are ready for the way out.
Leave the Alcazaba and cross the Plaza de los Aljibes.
Pass the Wine Gate, and follow the signs south to the great gate in the southern wall, the Puerta de la Justicia.
That is stop twenty.

tracks.title: Stop 20. Out by the Puerta de la Justicia

segments.text: Stop twenty.
Out by the Puerta de la Justicia.
You are inside the walls, in front of the great gate in the southern wall.
This is the Puerta de la Justicia, the Gate of Justice.
If it is open as an exit, it is your way out.
Do not hurry through it.
Stop first, facing the inner arch.
Look up, above the inner arch.
A key is carved there.
You saw the same key earlier, on the Wine Gate.
Now look above the key.
In a niche stands a Gothic Virgin and Child.
This one is a copy.
The original was carved in fifteen oh one and is attributed to Roberto Alemán.
It is the statue you heard about in the museum, upstairs in the Palace of Charles the Fifth.
Now find the Arabic writing.
This is the foundation inscription.
It dates the gate to thirteen forty-eight, under Yusuf the First.
Stones that record a building's founding like this are rare in the Alhambra.
Look also for an inscription inlaid in white marble from Macael, set with slate.
It is the only documented use of that technique anywhere in the Alhambra.
Think about what you are looking at.
The Catholic Monarchs set their Virgin over a sultan's foundation inscription.
It is the layering of conquest you have seen all day, in one small space.
The gate's Arabic name is Bab al-Sharia.
It is usually translated as the Gate of the Esplanade, and sometimes as the Gate of the Law.
Now walk slowly through the passage.
Count the arches as you pass under them.
Look at the great wooden door.
It is the original, sheathed in metal.
Often told, and only partly confirmed.
The passage is usually described as a bent entrance.
It turns at right angles, so that attackers could not charge straight through.
Watch for the turns as you walk.
We could not confirm how many there are.
When you are outside, turn around and face the gate.
Look up, to the stone at the very top of the great outer arch, the keystone.
An open hand is carved on it.
A myth check on the hand and the key.
Both are Islamic symbols, and their exact meaning is debated.
The hand is popularly read as the five pillars of Islam, or as a charm against the evil eye.
You will hear that judges once held court under this gate.
There is no record to support it.
And there is the legend Washington Irving retells.
The Alhambra will stand until the hand reaches down and grasps the key.
On that day, the whole fortress will fall.
The hand is out here, and the key is on the inner arch.
They have not met yet.
One last thing you will hear.
The fountain of Charles the Fifth, beside the gate, is said to carry the arms of Burgundy and Lorraine among its imperial heraldry.
That too is thinly sourced.
From here the path drops through the woods to the Cuesta de Gomérez, and down to the Plaza Nueva in the city.
If you need the Access Pavilion, for a bus or a car, go back through the gate instead.
Walk east along the Calle Real and the Cypress Walk.
It takes about twenty minutes.
Before you go, there is one last track, the closing.
Play it here, or on the way down the hill.

tracks.title: Closing

segments.text: Closing.
What you have walked through.
You began in a council chamber, and you have ended at a fortress gate.
In between, you saw how one dynasty built a public stage, a private paradise and a country estate.
All three were fed by one channel of mountain water.
You also saw what came after.
Chapels, an emperor's palace, the Romantic writers, and the restorers who put the lions back.
Much of what you saw has been repaired or rebuilt, from the ceiling of the Sala de la Barca to the jets of water in the Generalife.
That does not make the surviving Nasrid work less remarkable.
It makes it more so.
In nineteen eighty-four, the Alhambra and the Generalife were named a World Heritage site by UNESCO.
Ten years later, the Albaicín, the old quarter across the valley, was added.
Remember, too, the people this guide has not named.
They are the labourers who rammed the earth, cut the tiles and carved the plaster.
They worked by hand, with ropes and pulleys and no machines.
We celebrate the sultans.
But the walls are the labourers' work.
If you have time, you can follow the Nasrids down the hill.
The Dobla de Oro ticket adds a set of Nasrid monuments in the Albaicín.
Check what it includes when you buy.
Before you head down the hill, turn and look back at the red walls.
The motto carved inside them says that there is no victor but God.
The sultans lost their city in fourteen ninety-two.
What they built is still standing.
Thank you for walking with us.
